title: Factory children
sentences: It is winter.
A cold December night, with chill fingers, holds the blindfold over the eyes of old Holland's grey university town.
Only a worthy companion of this century's giant spirit wages war with the night and repeatedly tears the blindfold away.
Look: gas flames cast a fleeting light from distance to distance into the hollow streets, and yonder along the sombre canals.
What is that camp for; what is that light for?
For the city has gone to rest and sleeps—or so one might think.
Do not believe it, for again and again she must wake and see,
wake and see to keep watch against the disaster that might approach.
And the old city does not sleep either.
Only at times is she seized by a light slumber,
and it seems to you as though she dreamed of her ancient fame—like the tender bough on the grey monarch of the Alps,
that gently dozes upon her breast, and murmurs and whispers of the greatness of its origin.
Yet however fleeting her slumber—ever peering over the blindfold,
to keep watch even in the night—she cannot manage it as she would wish.
The poor town is ill!
Yes, the head is clear, even clearer than before; yes, her heart beats as loudly for virtue and fidelity as in the days of her youth,
and yet you see well enough how her right arm lies there as if paralysed.
Listen:
Part of her noblest sap has passed into impure humours; humours that have formed a repulsive wound;
a wound that consumes her strength and in the end will lead her to the ruin of her glorious existence.
Poor city!

feverishly his blood raced through his veins, for you see—they have shown him that wound!

Was it any wonder that he had difficulty at once striking the right tone, aware of the high weight of his calling.

Yet our task is not finished thereby.
We still have two scenes.
The first you see in a fair yet fantastical light; the second in the deep black of night,
when only a single star breaks through the driven clouds.
And that first tableau.
See, in that dazzling art-light, lovely as moonshine, bright as the sun, gleaming as gold and silver intermingled,
there you see, amid a laughing garden, a youth; you recognise him at once; it is the alert nobleman
who equips himself with knowledge to watch later over the rights of humanity; it is Willem van Hogenstad.
At his side stands a tender yet charming little boy, neatly and brightly dressed,
amid the wealth and splendour of a nature hitherto unknown to him,
lifting his eyes again and again to his benefactor with the expression of the most grateful delight and the deepest attachment.
That little boy is the poor factory child, the child of Zwarte; the lad who through the power of money was rescued from his wretched state,
and will be reared and taught to become a man—a true man!
It is a pity that such an art-light passes so quickly.
The beautiful scene has vanished.
We stand in darkness, in night's black.
Do you hear yonder—there in that dark corner—that plaintive little voice.
It wails
for—water.....
water!
Countless times you hear it: water!
And then, when the little voice grows weary of always the same word, it groans: Thirst, thirst!
Parents!
do you not hear your child.
Mother Zwarte, do you not know that your poor Saartje, with burning lips and tongue,
longs for a draught, and is too weak to fetch it herself?
But the mother—she sleeps; and the father—he snores.
Before going to bed the drunken man had said
that he knew these tricks well and—if she was too lazy for her work, she might just let herself be picked up by some fine gentleman, like Sander; that paid better.
And the mother had thought it would not be so bad if she could only get properly warm;
and she tucked the shivering girl in a little better with a skirt she had taken off when going to bed.
When the mother had done that, then a small, a very small star shone between the black clouds.
But now, now it is night again, pitch-dark night;
for the storm wind has also extinguished the gas flame that still burned not far from Zwarte's dwelling.
And there sleep the parents who, even if from low self-interest alone,
should have kept watch at the bed of their mortally ill child.
And that child—it can no longer say it is thirsty; her lips are as if scorched;
her little mouth burns within; in her little head it pounds and roars and drones.
That is the fever, the hot devouring fever.
Such a poor weakened creature is not able to withstand that fever.
And—no one hears her ever softer and duller moaning.
And no one sees the clammy sweat pearling on the dull little face; and no one hears—no!
no one hears, after six hours' struggle, that last, that very last soft painful sob, the sob that sounds like a grateful sweet-flowing.....
deliverance!
And outside, the storm wind bellows as with thunderous echo: Murdered!
murdered!
And that, that is now the wound of the poor university town.
It is hideous!
You understand now that it is an urgent plea for medicine with which the messenger charged himself.
A request?
No, a supplication; for he
is not the first messenger; he only urges haste.
Murdered!
Murdered!
bellows the wind.
And yes, those poor factory children—they are murdered in soul and body.
In a new form I gave you that old, but all the more terrible truth.
Only what I myself saw or heard, or also learned from eyewitnesses, I gave you back in swift strokes.
And that my tale has not satisfied you, that you found it 'not beautiful'—see, that would rejoice me,
if I had only struck you; if you only felt deeply that yonder are fellow creatures, weak children, poorly clothed and wretchedly fed,
who must work thirteen, fourteen, fifteen hours a day in a small space—yes, sometimes moreover the entire long night before the Sunday that must follow.
And a great part of those unhappy creatures—they are the breadwinners for their lazy merciless parents, they are....
But indeed, I have sketched them for you, sketched them truthfully although I did not speak of the far-reaching immorality that surrounds them infectiously;
and if you do not believe me: well then, visit the Leiden factories; you will see and, if your heart does not
bleed at once, then, then surely—returned to your dwelling,
at the sight of your dear blooming offspring, you must cry out: Great God!
does such a dreadful evil exist in our beloved Netherlands,
in the land whose grand past speaks of freedom and of justice for all!
Good God, is nothing done in our dear fatherland for those hundreds,
yes thousands of wretched ones who are murdered there, yes murdered!
And even if those miserable parents are also excusable, yes innocent if you will—ignorant, enervated beings as they themselves mostly were from youth;
and even if many of the factory owners look down with compassion upon the misery that surrounds them; even if many upright honest men among them give you the sincere assurance
that they too fervently wish to be able to lift those poor ones somewhat from the pitiable state in which they live,
they whisper to you: 'What we want, we cannot; there is one who prevents us, and her name is: Competition!'
How!
would she be the murderess of those poor children, she the fair sturdy woman who bears the motto of freedom on her banner?
Yes, it is she!
And the fair woman who bathes herself in
the incense odours wafted toward her—she sins, stupefied, through that scent.
Her motto of freedom—she carries it high, shamelessly high.
'Freedom!
yes freedom for all and everything!'
she shrieks in mad arrogance: 'Who shall deprive parents of their right over their children;
who shall command them to lighten their labour or send them to school; who—who shall prevent me.......'
Be silent, fair madwoman.
Do you not know how the State—and justly—deprives the poor fallen woman
who out of shame murdered her child of freedom, thank God, only rarely of her life?
Ha!
for that unhappy one the prison, and for you the wildest freedom;
you who consort with gold-lust and murder thousands of children, murder without blushing in soul and body.
No!
I tell you, the hour will soon strike when you will be imprisoned, yes imprisoned in the bonds of a blessed law!
Illustrious Sovereign!
Mighty legislators of the State!
See, there the supplication falls down before your feet.
the sick city and her sisters—they long for deliverance and medicine.
You do not ask the messenger where the herb is
to be found, the herb that can give help.
You know well: Yonder, on the other side of the Ocean, there it blooms and thrives on England's soil;
there a fair blessed law protects those poor, poor factory children from the wretched state in which they live here.
There their working hours are fewer; there they go to school and are taught, three, yes five hours per day.
And the instructed children become skilled workers, and industry flourishes there; and I ask you,
why should we lag behind our overseas neighbours, yes even behind most of the less developed States of Europe?
But why do I speak of seeking medicine abroad;
your wisdom will know how to find it on native soil, according to native needs.
No, I ask you for nothing more than a law in the interest of those unfortunates.
The scene I sketched of the noble boy with the little lad at his side—it was placed in an art-light.
That picture might be an exception; a future for those poor ones it cannot become.
Those indigent children—they must work and they will and can if you take pity on them;
yes they will do more than now, for now they are
paralysed and enervated, and experience elsewhere has taught that excessive labour in industry becomes harmful,
while more rest and instruction for those little ones powerfully elevates them.
O, Illustrious Sovereign!
and Mighty legislators of the State!
do not believe the false messengers, should they come,
who would tell you that the help we beg from you is unnecessary.
'They would lie!'
But no, they will not come; for I tell you: They,
they would in truth be the wretched ones who seduced the fair woman to debauchery and child-murder.
Those messengers—yes, they would turn pale if you powerfully charged them that they are indeed the murderers of our poor factory children.
No, none will come there
who would boldly throw in your face that no murder takes place in the full sense of the word.
I beg you, let me deal with him who would dare to try; I then ask him gently: Tell me, unhappy one,
have you then forgotten that one little room, the room with the cleaning machine for raw cotton,
beside which the child in only a few years sacrifices its wretched life of weariness—let it sound softer—to weariness?
See—see, then he turns pale and slinks away.
But I know it—there will, there can come no messengers to testify against my mission.
Listen, listen!
the poor city wails too loudly and groans from the pain.
Illustrious Sovereign!
Noble and Mighty legislators of the State!
See: upon your garments and mine, upon which the little hands of those children worked,
drops of blood cling; yes the drops of blood of the poor murdered factory children in the Netherlands.
O!
delay then not a moment longer, send the help that you can command; it is urgent, greatly urgent.
Raise the city from her distress, and her sisters with her; and then, then a voice will sigh through your souls:
'Blessed are you that you have worked together—not for alleviation, but to prevent misery and woe;
blessed are you that you have secured a fairer future for Dutch Industry; and blessed are you, blessed above all,
that you have rescued yonder those poor ones—and now without payment—in soul and body, and truly have loved them.
